Transcript:
[00:00] Maya: Hey everyone, thanks for joining. This is Maya from Redwood, I'm the AE on the partnership. We have Jordan our SE and Liam on the line too. How are you all doing?
[00:08] Rajesh: Good, thanks. Excited to learn more. Helena and Ethan on my side, plus Sofia for the security bits.
[00:15] Maya: Great. Quick agenda, we'll do intros, go over SummitGate's goals for a partner integration, talk about the technical touchpoints we typically see, and then outline pilot and GTM possibilities. Jordan will cover technical patterns.
[00:26] Jordan: Hi all, Jordan Park, Redwood SE. I'll try not to nerd out too fast but will sketch the runtime and how we think about hybrid placements — hosted vs dedicated vs private.
[00:36] Helena: For context, SummitGate runs a managed hybrid cloud platform focused on telco and enterprise customers, we operate colo sites and public cloud peering. We're exploring strategic partners to offer inference-as-a-service at the edge and in customer VPCs.
[00:50] Maya: Awesome. High level, Redwood provides a unified inference runtime you can surface as hosted API, dedicated pools, or a private deployment in the customer VPC. For partners we typically integrate in two ways: 1) co-managed deployment where Redwood's control plane connects to a SummitGate managed cluster, or 2) a reseller model where SummitGate bundles Redwood Dedicated capacity under a commercial arrangement.
[01:12] Rajesh: Ok that maps to what we were thinking. A few constraints up front: some customers require on-prem, or air-gapped; others want predictable SLAs in region. We also have strict KMS and key custody requirements for certain regulated customers.
[01:27] Jordan: Totally — we've seen that. Our Private offering can be deployed in a VPC with customer-managed networking and KMS integrations. For air-gapped, there's a packaged on-prem option. One nuance: kernel-level optimizations and quantized runtimes differ by GPU families, so if you're running A100 vs H100 vs Ampere alternatives there are perf tradeoffs we can help characterize.
[01:48] Ethan: Quick question — what telemetry do you require back to Redwood control plane? We need to be explicit for our security team.
[01:55] Jordan: Good call. For Private we can limit telemetry to heartbeats and anonymized usage metrics; everything else can be pushed to SummitGate's observability stack. We support S3-style log sinks and event streaming to Kafka.
[02:08] Sofia: And about audit logs and key rotation — do you support customer-managed CMKs?
[02:12] Jordan: Yes, KMS integrations exist. We can support customer CMKs and HSM-based key custody in the private package, logs are configurable to meet SOC2 requirements. We'll include the exact artifact set in the security checklist.
[02:24] Maya: On the go-to-market side, Helena, we often do co-sell pilots with a revenue share or committed capacity discounts for partner-resold Dedicated. There's flexibility — some partners prefer listed pricing with referral fees, others want a private reseller SKU.
[02:39] Helena: We're leaning toward a reseller SKU plus co-marketing for the initial 6-month run. Procurement will want clear MSA terms.
[02:46] Liam: We can draft a short partner MSA outline. Usually it covers data residency, SLAs, support response times, and termination. We can reuse Redwood's partner MSA as a starting point.
[02:58] Rajesh: From a tech pilot POV, we want to validate latency at the colo sites for a 4k token LLM and run an embedding workload. That will give us the token throughput numbers we need to size pools.
[03:12] Jordan: Good, we can do that. Two typical pilot modes: 1) deploy Redwood Private in your colo with a small GPU pool and run the model container (bring-your-own model or Redwood-curated open model), or 2) route traffic from SummitGate's managed tenants to Redwood Dedicated in our cloud and test routing/latency.
[03:30] Ethan: The first is preferable for end customers that require data residency, but we need to test the cost delta. How do you measure per-token cost in a Dedicated/reseller setup?
[03:40] Maya: We'll share a unit economics sheet, but generally: tokens are measured at the API layer and translated to instance-hour costs plus GPU amortization; Dedicated/reseller SKUs can have a fixed committed capacity component plus overage. Jordan will follow up with a benchmark plan to estimate TCO.
[03:55] Jordan: On benchmarks, we'll need a sample model (container or HF model name), sequence length distribution, and concurrency profile. We'll provide a spreadsheet that asks for those inputs.
[04:09] Helena: We'll pull that together. Also, marketing — we want to co-brand a launch if pilot succeeds, webinars, and maybe a joint case study.
[04:18] Maya: Sounds good. We'll include a GTM proposal with co-marketing options.
[04:24] [05:00] (brief hold/music)
[05:08] Rajesh: A couple technical clarifications — how do you handle KV cache when moving requests between regions or model variants? We worry about warm caches and cold starts causing poor latency.
[05:18] Jordan: We use a combination of prefix-level caching and warm pools. When we route between compatible model variants, there is a warmup plan; for strict low-latency SLOs we recommend colocated private pools or dedicated pinned instances. There's also streaming and chunking options to mask cold starts.
[05:35] Ethan: Is there an edge runtime that can live on SummitGate nodes with minimal footprint? Some of our colo hardware is older.
[05:42] Jordan: Yes, we support quantized runtimes and a lightweight inference agent that ships as a container. It will have lower memory/perf limits; for heavy gen you'd want a modern GPU. For older GPUs we can fall back to CPU for embeddings but with degraded latency.
[05:57] Sofia: From compliance — we will need SOC2 Type II report, penetration test summary, and encryption-in-transit proofs. Is that standard?
[06:05] Maya: Absolutely, we can share SOC2 and pen test artifacts under an NDA and include a security checklist for the pilot. We'll also highlight the KMS integration docs.
[06:15] Rajesh: What's the expected uplift if we run in colo vs Redwood hosted? Rough ballpark, like 2x cost but better latency?
[06:23] Jordan: It depends on utilization and GPU type. Running in dedicated colo nodes can be more expensive on an absolute basis but the latency and data residency benefits are often worth it. Our Optimize toolkit gives suggestions on quantization and batching to reduce token cost — sometimes 30-60% improvements depending on workload.
[06:40] Helena: Commercially, we need a partner SKU that allows us to predict monthly spend for a customer. Variable billing makes procurement difficult.
[06:48] Maya: Understood. For reseller partner setups we can do committed capacity blocks with an uplift to cover SummitGate margin, and transparent per-token overage pricing. We'll draft some examples.
[06:58] Liam: I'd like to flag network egress considerations. If you're serving from colo to external customers, egress costs and peering arrangements will matter. We can work with SummitGate on traffic routing patterns to minimize surprises.
[07:11] Ethan: Good point. We'll map peering and cost centers.
[07:15] Jordan: Another technical note: we can ship a validation container that runs a small synthetic workload to validate perf and correctness before a pilot. That usually helps unblock infra teams.
[07:27] Rajesh: Great. On timeline, we're aiming to have a pilot framework early Q1 2026, ideally a proof-of-latency and embeddings validation in January. Does that align?
[07:36] Maya: Yes, that's doable. We'll coordinate calendar availability.
[07:40] Helena: On partner economics there are three things to decide: reseller SKU pricing, committed capacity discounts, and marketing co-investment. We'll need examples to present to our GTM and finance teams.
[07:52] Maya: We'll include an example financial model in the follow-up.
[07:56] [08:10] (Jordan shares screen briefly to show architecture diagram — audible clicks)
[08:15] Jordan: Here's a rough flow: SummitGate tenant calls into either a customer VPC deployment of Redwood Private or a SummitGate-provisioned Dedicated pool. Requests are routed by policy — latency-first for colo, cost-first for hosted. Observability feeds into both Redwood Console and SummitGate's logging.
[08:35] Ethan: When you say 'route by policy' — is that something we control, or is it Redwood control plane decisioning?
[08:41] Jordan: Policy is configurable. SummitGate and the end-customer can set routing policies; partners can also enforce default routing via the partner control plane. We'll outline how policy precedence works in the runbook.
[08:54] Sofia: A security wrinkle — what authentication flows do you support for cross-account calls? We need to ensure no long-lived secrets are exposed in transit.
[09:02] Jordan: We support short-lived tokens, mutual TLS, and role-based assumptions for cross-account. We also have SAML SSO support for the console-level access.
[09:12] Rajesh: Ok, that's promising. Any major blockers you foresee?
[09:17] Maya: Nothing insurmountable. The usual items: aligning procurement/MSA, sorting the KMS/HSM key custody in pilot, and deciding on pilot infrastructure (colo vs dedicated). All of those are procedural, not technical blockers.
[09:31] Helena: What about training for our support teams? We need documentation and runbooks.
[09:36] Liam: We'll provide partner onboarding docs, runbooks, and a short enablement workshop. Typically a half-day technical workshop plus a biz/ops GTM session.
[09:47] Rajesh: For the pilot, we need the following from Redwood: benchmark plan, sample container or model names, security checklist, rough pricing examples. From our side, we'll provide sample traffic profiles, a target colo site, and procurement timeline.
[10:02] Maya: Yes — Jordan will take the benchmark lead; Maya will handle GTM and commercial; Liam will handle enablement and MSA draft.
[10:12] Jordan: I'll send the benchmark spreadsheet after the call; please fill in model name, sequence lengths, QPS expectations. We'll do a capacity estimate and an initial perf run in our staging cluster.
[10:23] Helena: If we do a co-sell pilot and it scales, is there an SLA you offer partners?
[10:29] Maya: For Dedicated and Private customers we have SLA-backed targets for uptime and latency tiers depending on the contract. We can map those to a partner offering.
[10:37] Ethan: Any pre-existing partners you've done this with that have a similar colo model?
[10:41] Maya: We've done a handful with regional cloud and colo partners — we can share anonymized case studies. We'll include one that shows latency gains in a colo deployment.
[10:49] Rajesh: Pricing orientation — for committed capacity do you offer true-up or committed minimums only?
[10:55] Maya: Both. We can structure a committed minimum with negotiated true-up thresholds, or a consumption-first reseller SKU with fixed margins for SummitGate. We'll provide examples.
[11:06] Sofia: Security again — for the pilot we'll likely need to run an NDA and then you'll provide SOC2 docs. Is that the normal sequence?
[11:13] Maya: Yes, NDA → SOC2 and pentest artifacts → pilot security checklist. We'll start the NDA immediately if you want.
[11:21] Helena: Yes please. We'll route NDA to legal.
[11:24] Maya: I'll send both the NDA and the partner one-pager after this call.
[11:29] Rajesh: Any other technical constraints we haven't covered?
[11:33] Jordan: One more — model quantization and kernel availability for certain GPU drivers can affect perf. If you have mixed hardware across colo sites we'll need to plan model families per hardware class to avoid mismatches.
[11:46] Ethan: We do have mixed racks, yes. We'll identify candidate racks for the pilot that have H100 or A100 equivalents.
[11:55] Maya: Good. Let's capture clear next steps.
[12:00] [12:15] (recap)
[12:18] Maya: Recap — Redwood to: 1) send partner runbook and NDA; 2) Jordan sends benchmark spreadsheet and requests sample model/container; 3) Redwood to draft partner MSA outline and a pricing example; 4) SummitGate to identify pilot colo site, provide traffic profile, and route NDA to legal.
[12:40] Helena: We will do that and get back with dates for the tech deep dive first week of January.
[12:47] Rajesh: Sounds good. Appreciate the time.
[12:50] Maya: Thanks everyone. We'll follow up with a calendar invite for the technical deep dive and attach the runbook.
[12:58] (meeting ends)
